newsitem.title: RUSSIA: No dramatic improvement in Yeltsin health - Kremlin.
newsitem.headline: No dramatic improvement in Yeltsin health - Kremlin.

text.p: Doctors treating Boris Yeltsin said on Friday the Russian president was breathing more easily after his admission to hospital with pneumonia but there had been no dramatic improvement in his condition, the Kremlin said.
Yeltsin, 65, was taken to hospital on Wednesday just two weeks after returning to work in the Kremlin following major heart surgery.

"The president is breathing with more ease, there are less crepitations in his lungs. The temperature remains normal, blood pressure is stable," the Kremlin said in a statement issued after morning checks by doctors.
"But at the same time doctors think it is too early to speak about a breakthrough," it said.

A Kremlin spokeswoman declined to comment on a report on Moscow's Ekho Moskvy radio station quoting hospital sources as saying Yeltsin was suffering from an inflammation "of medium gravity" of both lungs.

Yeltsin, who had heart bypass surgery on November 5, was taken to the Central Clinical Hospital in Moscow two days ago with what the Kremlin initially described as the first signs of pneumonia. It described his condition as pneumonia on Thursday but gave few details.
Russian markets appeared calm over Yeltsin's illness and top shares opened higher after the Russian Trading System set a record on Thursday.
But many newspapers painted a picture of a leaderless country.
"President Sick, Premier On Holiday, Country All On Its Own", said a headline in the mainstream liberal Izvestia.
The Kremlin, anxious to portray Yeltsin as still engaged in state affairs, said on Thursday that the president was in telephone contact with a number of Russian and foreign leaders.
It said he might speak to German Chancellor Helmut Kohl later on Friday.
The Kremlin has played down Yeltsin's condition and insists it has nothing to do with his quintuple heart bypass operation.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin's constitutional deputy, was confident enough to begin a planned week's holiday near Moscow. He spoke by telephone to Yeltsin, who is being treated with antibiotics.

Chernomyrdin, who would assume power for up to three months before elections if the president were to step down, spent six months effectively running the country after Yeltsin suffered a bout of heart trouble shortly before his re-election on July 3.
It was not clear how long Yeltsin may be in hospital.
